target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce school/work barriers enough to improve voting access
objection: A federal “national holiday” designation does not, by itself, require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many private-sector workers could still be scheduled to work or lose pay on Election Day.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would help low-income workers broadly
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately concentrated in private-sector hourly jobs such as retail and service work, where paid holidays are less reliably granted, so the burden of a holiday-only approach would fall unevenly on them.

target: AG1’s conclusion that the holiday would remove practical voting obstacles
objection: If low-income workers must work or lose wages on Election Day, then a holiday does not reliably reduce their voting obstacles and can create new barriers through lost pay and reduced flexibility.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would be an effective turnout booster
objection: Research indicates that creating an election-day holiday by itself is not an effective strategy for increasing turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s broader policy conclusion that a holiday should be the main response
objection: A policy that can disadvantage low-income workers and is not a reliable turnout lever should not be adopted at the federal level when more reliable approaches exist, such as state laws requiring employer time off for voting or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday label alone would not guarantee time off or prevent wage loss
objection: A national Election Day holiday policy can include job-protected time to vote or guaranteed time off, which would prevent the wage-loss barrier the opponent highlights, including for low-income hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not meaningfully reduce scheduling conflicts
objection: Millions of Americans also face school-day obligations and childcare-related conflicts; pausing normal school obligations on Election Day would free up time for many voters even if some employers remain open.

target: AG2’s view that a federal holiday is ineffective because it lacks a specific paid-leave mandate
objection: A federal holiday designation would still change workplace expectations and operating patterns for many employers, leading to fewer staffed shifts and reduced hours, which would reduce rigid work scheduling even without a separate paid-leave statute.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is unreliable simply because it is a legal label
objection: The reliability concern wrongly treats the holiday approach as only a legal label; in practice, many comparable democracies already hold elections on weekends or holidays, showing the model can work operationally.

target: AG1’s reliance on foreign election-day holidays/weekends as proof of U.S. feasibility
objection: Other democracies’ weekend or holiday elections do not show that a U.S. federal holiday would reliably guarantee job-protected time to vote for low-income workers, because federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that celebratory framing makes the holiday a sufficient turnout reform
objection: Civic motivation or celebratory framing cannot substitute for removing the practical day-of constraints that prevent constrained voters from voting; if those barriers remain, turnout will not reliably improve for the most constrained groups.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday addresses the main access problem
objection: Election access barriers also include administrative eligibility and registration steps that a holiday does not address, so reducing only day-of scheduling conflicts is insufficient as a broad election-access reform.

target: AG1’s assumption that day-of scheduling barriers are the central obstacle for all voters
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably remove the wage-loss or inflexible-scheduling bottleneck for low-income hourly workers, who are the group most likely to face the greatest practical constraints.

target: AG1’s inference from other countries that holiday elections are workable in the U.S.
objection: Many countries that hold elections on non-working days do so with labor institutions or other protections that make those days truly non-work for large parts of the workforce, whereas a U.S. federal holiday would not automatically create those protections for private hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would not reliably disadvantage low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not legally compel private employers to close or provide paid time off, so low-income workers in hourly retail and service jobs can still be required to work during voting hours or lose wages, making the policy unequally burdensome.

target: AG2’s objection that holiday status is merely symbolic and does not change workplace norms
objection: A national holiday is not just symbolic in practice; it changes day-of school and work norms because schools and many workplace routines pause or operate on reduced schedules, reducing scheduling conflicts that block voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a widely observed holiday would not harm low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday designation does not legally require private employers to close or provide paid leave, so employer staffing discretion and workers’ wage-loss risk remain largely unchanged, leaving low-income hourly workers exposed to work-day voting barriers.

target: AG2’s underlying assumption that holiday status will not alter workplace behavior enough to matter
objection: The opponent’s harm case depends on assuming a holiday is only a label, but making Election Day a national holiday would frame voting as a civic celebration and change workplace expectations so employers and communities are more likely to support participation.
